6.3 Operating phases used in the plans

The year is organised into nine operating phases that follow the stages above: (1) Rest and winter pruning; (2) Bud break and inflorescence growth; (3) Flowering; (4) Fruit set and first fruit growth; (5) Pit hardening; (6) Fruit growth and oil accumulation; (7) Maturation and harvest monitoring; (8) Harvest; (9) Post-harvest. Plan weeks are assigned to these phases from the monthly timing in the sources, so week numbers carry Low confidence unless the source gives the date itself. Phases 6–9 differ between the three types.

7.2 Planting material and propagation

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Infected nursery plants have spread Verticillium wilt to orchards worldwide; the EPPO PM 4/17 scheme produces tested trees and rootstocks free of Verticillium, Xylella and ArMV, CLRV and SLRSV viruses.[58]Medium
2Xylella fastidiosa is absent from Egypt, which temporarily suspended imports of fruit-tree seedlings from infected countries.[59]Medium
3Leafy sub-terminal cuttings under mist, vapour-pressure-deficit control or in wooden boxes, with IBA at 4,000 ppm (North Sinai).[13]High
4Under mist and VPD control June was the best date (mean 38%) and December the worst (about 9%); in wooden boxes March was best, with the highest rate 86% for Chiperssino in March.[13]High
5Wooden boxes gave the highest rooting percentage, while intermittent mist used the most water.[13]High
6In the Horticulture Research Institute trial (mist, IBA 5,000 ppm for 5 seconds), April was the best date, then October, with January the worst.[18]High
7IBA is not listed in Annex I (plant protection) or Annex II (fertilisers) of Regulation 2021/1165; check with the certifier before using it in an organic nursery.[55]Medium
8Rootstocks that prevent fungal proliferation (resistant) such as Frantoio are more effective against wilt than tolerant rootstocks when Picual is grafted on them, but a susceptible scion increases the rootstock's susceptibility.[60]High

7.3 Site preparation

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Assess the soil to at least 1 m by opening profiles and sampling; favourable values: depth over 0.8 m, loam to clay-loam texture, good drainage, pH 5.5–8.5 (optimum 6.0–7.5), P2O5 over 25 mg/kg, K2O over 50 mg/kg.[56]Medium
2Loosen the soil to about 1 m without inverting the layers (ripping, then a chisel or tine cultivator), and clear hard-to-control weeds before planting.[56]Medium
3Verticillium microsclerotia survive in soil for up to 14 years; crop rotation is not adequate because of the fungus's wide host range; soil solarisation and organic amendments help manage it.[60]High
4Olive grows on any well-drained, aerated soil with pH 6.5–8.5 and needs a 1.0–1.5 m soil profile; avoid sites with groundwater shallower than 1.2 m or standing water; olive is affected at an exchangeable sodium percentage of 20–40.[36]Medium
5Pre-planting soil correction: alkaline soil is acidified with elemental sulphur (450–900 kg/ha for sandy soil, 1.8–2.25 t for clay) in two applications a year apart; sodic soil is corrected with gypsum followed by leaching of the sodium.[36]Medium
6Solarisation is explicitly listed among preventive methods in the organic regulation.[53]High

7.4 Planting time and hole preparation

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1The most suitable planting time in Egypt is from mid-February to mid-May, with a second window from mid-August to mid-November.[61]Low
2The best time is March and April, then autumn (September and October), avoiding the hot months (June–August) and frost (December and January).[62]Low
3Planting time: year round, except July–August and November–January.[36]Medium
4Planting-hole mix of about 15 kg compost with superphosphate and sulphur; the hole is irrigated twice before planting.[62]Low
5Superphosphate is not on the list of permitted fertilisers; the listed alternative is soft ground rock phosphate, and elemental sulphur is listed.[55]High

8. Newly Planted Seedlings: Operations and Plan to the Onset of Fruiting

8.1 Scope of this section

This section covers the seedling from preparation before planting to the onset of fruiting. In Egypt olive is propagated mainly by rooted cuttings (Section 7.2), so the section deals with a rooted or grafted nursery plant ready for planting. Numbers are taken from the sources; where no published number exists this is listed in Section 13.

8.2 Planting material ready for the field

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Organic planting material is used; non-organic plants need authorisation from the control body before planting, for one season at a time, and must not be treated with non-permitted products.[53]High
2Prefer plants produced under the EPPO PM 4/17 scheme, tested for Verticillium, Xylella and viruses.[58]Medium
3Cutting-grown trees bear fruit in about four years; the cultivar can be changed by bark grafting or top-working.[36]Medium
4Start of bearing: Toffahi is early; Aggezi Shami and Hamed are intermediate.[2] [3]High

8.3 Irrigation and nutrition of the young tree

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Irrigate with water only for the first one or two weeks, then apply fertiliser with every irrigation at an N:K ratio of 1:1 once the trees show signs of establishment.[63]Medium
2Nitrogen rate for young orchards: 1 g N per tree per day for every year of age.[63]Medium
3In organic production mineral nitrogen fertiliser is banned, so nitrogen comes only from permitted sources.[53] [55]High
4In the first year after planting, fertilisation and irrigation should be very frequent because the root system is small: fertilisation weekly or every two weeks and several irrigations per week depending on soil and environment, avoiding nutrient deficiency and water stress as well as over-irrigation and nitrogen over-fertilisation.[64]Medium
5The first-year doses in the US guide (urea, ammonium nitrate) are mineral fertilisers not permitted in organic production; only their frequency applies.[64] [53]High
6For young trees shading less than 60% of the ground: water need = reference ET × crop coefficient × reduction coefficient Kr = 2 × cover fraction; soil moisture or stem water potential monitoring is advised.[64]Medium
7Stem water potential: a non-stressed tree reads −11 bar on a mild spring day and −15 bar on a hot, dry day; mild stress is below −15 bar and medium stress between −20 and −25 bar.[64]Medium
8Recommended irrigation in the first two years: surface drippers.[36]Medium
9The crop coefficient is adjusted for the trees' ground cover; at 20% cover the basal coefficient falls to about 0.40.[65]High
10Boron for young trees: 10 g borax × years since planting, with care because it is toxic.[56]Medium

No.InformationSourceConfidence

    • Task 4: Borax 10 g × 2 years = 20 g per tree when needed. Source [56] · MediumHow often: Once (stated in source)
    • Task 5: Build the vase form for intensive orchards: trunk 80–100 cm and 2–4 main limbs inclined at 45–50°. Source [56] · MediumHow often: Not given in sources (not given in sources)
    • Task 6: Continue the year-1 protection programme (jasmine moth, bud mite, root rot). Source [66] [48] [51] · MediumHow often: According to monitoring (set by compiler from source timing)
    • Task 7: From month 12 of conversion: a single-ingredient product may be sold as 'in-conversion'. Source [53] · HighHow often: Once (stated in source)
  8. Year 3Transition to bearing
    • Task 1: Permitted fertiliser with every irrigation at 3 g N/tree/day. Source [63] · MediumHow often: With every irrigation (stated in source)
    • Task 2: Switch from surface drippers to subsurface drip. Source [36] · MediumHow often: Once (stated in source)
    • Task 3: Repeat leaf analysis every 1–2 years in July against the optimum ranges (Section 9.3); start phosphorus according to the analysis. Source [36] [56] · MediumHow often: Every 1–2 years (stated in source)
    • Task 4: Irrigate by the year-3 schedule (15–40 L per tree per day), then year 4 (30–60 L per tree per day). Source [36] · MediumHow often: Every 3–7 days (stated in source)
    • Task 5: Two copper sprays against olive knot: March and November. Source [70] · MediumHow often: Twice a year (stated in source)
    • Task 6: Start the olive fly programme once fruit appears (kaolin every two weeks from 1 June to harvest). Source [42] · HighHow often: Every two weeks (stated in source)
  9. Three years after conversion startedOnset of organic fruiting
    • Task 1: The first harvest that can be sold as organic comes after 3 full years of conversion; move to the weekly plan for bearing trees (Section 12). Source [53] [54] · HighHow often: Once (stated in source)
    • Task 2: Cutting-grown trees start bearing in about four years. Source [36] · MediumHow often: — (stated in source)
    • Task 3: In the Ismailia trial, Koroneiki, Coratina and Maraki yields were recorded in the fifth and sixth years after planting: 1.87–2.37 t/feddan (intensive) and 5.43–6.95 (super-high-density). Source [8] · HighHow often: — (stated in source)

9. Cultural Operations for Bearing Trees

9.1 Pruning

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Avoid heavy pruning of old trees because it weakens production; remove prunings and weeds from the farm, and burn branches infested with bark beetles (February recommendations).[69]Low
2Spray copper after pruning large trees (February recommendations).[69]Low
3Annual pruning improves light and aeration, reduces humidity and wetness periods inside the canopy, and improves spray penetration.[37]High
4In the California cost study the orchard is pruned in spring.[70]Medium
5The common form in intensive orchards is the vase: a trunk of 80–100 cm branching into 2–4 main limbs inclined at 45–50°.[56]Medium

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Leaf samples are taken in July: 100 leaves from non-bearing shoots.[73]Medium
2Recommended rates for a mature intensive orchard: nitrogen 150, phosphorus 35, potassium 200 kg/ha/year (from permitted sources in organic production).[64] [55]Medium
3Annual nitrogen about 0.5–1.5 kg/tree (50–150 kg/ha), needed most at fruit set (late April–mid-May), spring growth and fruit growth, applied with irrigation.[56]Medium
4Potassium is applied at a 2:1 ratio to nitrogen, especially in the year after a high-yield year.[56]Medium
5Boron: 100–150 g borax per mature tree every 4 years, and for young trees 10 g × years since planting; boron is toxic even at low concentrations.[56]Medium
6Nitrogen timing: in the root zone before growth and bloom (early spring–early summer); bearing-tree total 0.5–1.0 kg; when broadcast split half in January and half in October, and with fertigation apply about 25% after fruit set; excess before fruit set gives small fruit and more alternate bearing.[36]Medium
7Removal per tonne of fruit: 9.8 kg N, 25.9 kg P2O5, 12.4 kg K2O; annual tree uptake 276–578 g N and 200–560 g K2O in the producing countries.[36]Medium
8Many Mediterranean growers apply organic fertilisers every other year; top dressing with compost or composted manure needs careful balancing of nutrients; never place compost or fertiliser next to the trunk; feed lightly and often during the growing season.[36]Medium
9First leaf analysis at two years of age, then every 1–2 years, in July or 5–8 weeks after full bloom: 4 healthy leaves from the middle of current-season non-bearing shoots from 20–25 trees per block of up to 10 ha; for boron, mature fruit samples may be more reliable.[36]Medium
10Haifa programme for a fertigated bearing orchard (Spain, 500 trees/ha): N 200–300, P2O5 200–240, K2O 395–480 kg/ha; about two-thirds from spring to early summer and the rest after harvest; end fertigation 50 days before harvest; phosphorus by leaf analysis. (The fertilisers named are mineral; in organic production only the amounts and timing apply, from permitted sources.)[63] [53]Medium
11Olive-mill waste compost (wastewater and pomace) gave yields close to a commercial organo-mineral fertiliser in an organic grove over three years.[74]Medium
12In Picual, feldspar with a potassium-solubilising biofertiliser raised yield by up to 70%.[75]Low
13Potassium deficiency and excess nitrogen increase peacock spot.[37]High
14Phosphorus and potassium fertilisation in January if not applied in December.[76]Low

9.4 Soil, weed and cover-crop management

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1The regulation requires perennials to maintain fertility with short-term green manures, legumes and plant diversity, plus livestock manure or organic matter, preferably composted.[53]High
2Intercropping olive with chickpea or lentil raised soil organic matter without lowering olive yield (Morocco).[77]Medium
3Excessive weed growth reaching the lower canopy increases peacock spot; tillage or mowing reduces it.[37]High
4Shallow tillage about 10 cm deep in March to control weeds.[76]Low

10. Organic Pest and Disease Management

10.1 Olive fruit fly (Bactrocera oleae)

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1The fly has 3 to 6 generations a year; fruit becomes susceptible at pit hardening; a generation can be completed in 30–35 days in summer; it overwinters as pupae in soil or in fallen fruit.[56]Medium
2Yellow sticky traps caught more flies than McPhail traps; El-Behera was more affected than El-Fayoum.[78]Medium
3At Matrouh, McPhail traps showed two adult peaks during the fruit-free period: March and May.[79]Medium
4About 50% of eggs die on an 18–35 °C cycle, and none hatch at 18–37.8 °C (California).[80]Medium
5Kaolin (Super Nano) sprayed every 2 weeks from 1 June to harvest (12 sprays, 12–16 L per tree) at 3–5% reduced infestation by 69.3–83.4% at Matrouh; 5% was best and 3–4% more economical.[42]High
6Copper hydroxide reduced infestation by 55.9–59.9% and copper oxychloride by 48.0–58.5% (counts against the copper cap).[42] [55]High
7Food or pheromone traps for mass trapping are checked weekly in summer with the bait renewed regularly; they cut damage by 30–100%, but results vary and they are not enough alone.[56]Medium
8Spinosad bait (GF-120) applied weekly or every two weeks from late June to late October cut infestation to about 7% against 42.5% in the control (California); spinosad resistance was recorded there.[81]Medium
9Economic injury levels (Corfu) in females/McPhail trap/week: September 16 (25% of trees bearing) down to 4 (all trees bearing); October 6 down to 1.[82]Medium
10Reduce fallen fruit in which the insect overwinters, including sheep grazing before and after harvest; early harvest helps; mill as soon as possible after picking.[56]Medium
11Metarhizium brunneum sprayed under the canopy in autumn reduced the population by up to 50% (Spain).[83]Low

10.2 Olive moth (Prays oleae)

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Three generations in semi-arid Egyptian groves: flights in March–April, May–June and August–October; in arid groves the first two flights overlapped and no males were caught in August–October.[44]Medium
2Bt kurstaki: spray just before flowers open against the flower generation, just after fruit set against the fruit generation, and at the start of shoot growth against the leaf generation; time by population monitoring.[56]Medium
3Btk killed 86.6% of olive moth larvae in the lab.[68]Medium

10.3 Jasmine moth (Palpita unionalis)

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1A primary pest in nurseries and young irrigated plantings; mating disruption near Cairo targeted the first flight (May–June) and the second (September–November).[66]Medium
2Mating disruption with a two-component pheromone at 80 g a.i./ha gave about 90% male disorientation; the best Trichogramma result was several releases of 9,000 wasps per tree at two-week intervals.[66]Medium
3Four Trichogramma species occur naturally in Egyptian olive groves; monthly T. evanescens releases followed by a neem product were effective.[84]Medium
4Treat nurseries and young plantings when more than 5% of trees are infested in spring.[67]Low
5Btk killed 80.9% of jasmine moth larvae in the lab.[68]Medium

10.4 Olive psyllid (cotton insect)

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1The psyllid was recorded in Egypt in 1988 as a serious pest at Al-Arish and Rafah, and at Fayoum two years later.[45]High
2At Al-Arish (1997–1999): one generation a year; egg-laying starts in November in twig buds; nymphs appear from November/December and continue to June–August; peak around mid-April (about 60 nymphs per twig); adults all year with reproductive dormancy in summer and autumn.[45]High
3Damage: raceme drop, fewer flower buds and pistil drying, with honeydew causing sooty mould and drop of blossoms and young fruit; in Tunisia 6–8 insects per raceme caused 13% loss and over 30 insects more than 40% (Euphyllura olivina).[45]High
4Nymphs were most active at minimum temperatures of 13.3–13.9 °C and maximums of 25.3–26.3 °C; relative humidity (67.6–69.4%) was above the optimum range.[45]High
5In a nationwide survey the psyllid population peaked in March.[46]Medium
6Spray mineral oil at 1.5% against the olive cotton insect before bud break and the start of flowering (February recommendations).[69]Low
7Paraffin oils are on the list of substances permitted in organic production.[55]High

10.5 Scale insects

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Black scale: peaked in October, with Metaphycus lounsburyi parasitism of 34.2% and 40.1% in October.[46]Medium
2It thrives in humidity; canopy aeration by pruning and moderate irrigation are the first steps; control ants that protect it from parasitoids; for serious infestation spray paraffin oil in late July and, if needed, mid-August.[56]Medium
3Olive scale (Parlatoria oleae): releases of indigenous parasitoids raised parasitism without a visible fall in numbers.[85]Medium

10.6 Borers: leopard moth and bark beetle

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Leopard moth (Zeuzera pyrina): flight starts in mid-May and lasts until early November (northern Egypt).[86]Medium
2Mating disruption in heavily infested dense plantings reduced trap catches and active galleries and raised yield.[47]Medium
3Bark beetle: burn infested branches and remove prunings from the farm (February recommendations).[69]Low

10.7 Mites and nematodes

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Olive bud mite (Aceria oleae) is destructive on young trees, increasing 16.7-fold per 13.5-day generation at 31 °C and 80% RH; it is preyed on by Neoseiulus cydnodactylon and Agistemus olivi.[48]Medium
2Nematodes: in the field Nemastrol cut root-knot nematode by 82.4% and citrus nematode by 75.6% after 6 months; humic acid gave the best growth; abamectin cut nematodes by 85.4% in the greenhouse but is not on the list of organic-permitted substances.[49] [55]High

10.8 Peacock spot and olive knot

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Peacock spot: spores form at 5–25 °C, germination is optimal at 16–21 °C, and infection is optimal at about 20 °C with short wetness or 15 °C with long wetness; young leaves are also susceptible.[37]High
2Treatments are applied empirically in autumn and/or spring; in comparative trials (3–4 sprays in autumn and spring) copper hydroxide gave the best efficacy with the least metallic copper.[37]High
3Field-effective antagonists: Pseudomonas fluorescens, Bacillus atrophaeus and Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.[37]Medium
4Olive knot was first recorded in Egypt in Fayoum in 2008 and produced knots on Picual, Manzanillo and Frantoio within 20–30 days of inoculation.[50]Medium
5In the California cost study: one copper spray against knot in March in the first year, and from year three one in March and one in November.[70]Medium

10.9 Verticillium wilt and root rot

No.InformationSourceConfidence
136 isolates were taken from 12 sites in 8 regions of Egypt and fell into three vegetative compatibility groups (VCG2 dominant: 21 of 35 isolates).[43]High
2In the Mediterranean, incidence and symptom severity rise from late autumn–early winter to spring and drop sharply in summer; first symptoms in irrigated trees appear 18–24 months after planting in infested soil.[87]Medium
3Management: clean planting material, irrigation management, solarisation, organic amendments, biological control; chemical fumigation is ineffective or not allowed.[60]High
4Root rot in nurseries and new orchards in New Valley: 60.8% incidence and 48.7% severity in Dakhla, 52.1% and 43.6% in Kharga; Fusarium oxysporum the most frequent.[51]High
5Humic acid at 2.5 g/L as a soil drench gave the best protection, followed by Inicium, Fulvital and Bio-Health, all better than the chemical Rizolex-T.[51]High

10.10 Monitoring from satellite and drone imagery

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1With thermal drone imagery, crown-minus-air temperature rose about 2 K at low wilt severity, and the Crop Water Stress Index (CWSI) correlated with stomatal conductance (R² = 0.83); thermal resolution was 20 cm.[87]High
2Thermal indicators, visible ratios and fluorescence detected infection early, while structural indices such as NDVI related to visible damage.[87]High
3Combining weather data with Sentinel-2 NDVI reproduced relative soil water content to 1 m (r² = 0.795), after separating tree cover from grass; olive roots reach 0.8–1.0 m.[88]High

11.2 Organic olive oil

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1In Egypt more than 70% of oil is often extra virgin because picking is by hand and mill capacity exceeds the olive supply; 65% extra virgin and 15% virgin (2008/09).[2]High
2Irrigated oil olives give 14–18% oil at the mill, rainfed up to 22%.[2]High
3A known problem: Δ-7-stigmastenol and linolenic acid content in some Egyptian oils.[2]High
4Extra virgin limit 0.8% acidity; virgin up to 2%.[2]High

11.3 Organic table olives (green and black)

No.InformationSourceConfidence
1Sodium hydroxide is not permitted for olives in organic processing (only for sugar and plant oils other than olive oil), so organic table olives are the 'natural' type.[55] [54]High
2Natural olives are placed directly in brine where they ferment fully or partly; minimum salt 6%, maximum pH 4.3, minimum lactic acidity 0.3%.[1]High
3Heat treatment: pasteurisation of at least 15 pasteurisation units for natural olives.[1]High
4Trade categories Extra, First and Second; for example blemished green olives 4%, 6% and 10%; defects assessed on a sample of at least 200 fruits.[1]High
5Additives allowed by the international standard such as benzoate, sorbate and ferrous gluconate (to fix the colour of oxidised black olives) are not listed for organic products.[1] [55]High
6Acids permitted in organic processing: lactic, citric, tartaric, malic and ascorbic.[55]High

  • Task 2: Pit hardening is the most deficit-tolerant stage; in North Sinai irrigation at 80% ETc gave intermediate values and 60% the lowest, and alternate partial root-zone irrigation saved at least 20% of water. Source [56] [72] · MediumHow often: Not given in sources (not given in sources)
  • Task 3: Organic records: record every input, the reason for its use (proof of need) and the operations on each parcel. Source [53] [52] · HighHow often: With every operation (stated in source)
  • Task 4: Nitrogen: have it in the root zone just before the period of greatest uptake (ahead of shoot growth and bloom, early spring to early summer); without fertigation split into 4–6 applications from March to the end of June; with fertigation apply weekly amounts with at least 3 hours of irrigation, about 25% of the annual rate after fruit set; bearing-tree total 0.5–1.0 kg (0.5–1.5 kg in ECOLIVE); permitted organic sources only; excess before fruit set gives small fruit and more alternate bearing. Source [36] [63] [56] [53] · MediumHow often: 4–6 applications (March–June) or weekly by fertigation (stated in source)
  • Task 5: Haifa schedule for bearing orchards (over 10 t/ha, Mediterranean climate), early summer stage: pan evaporation 8.7 mm/day × coefficient 0.5 for oil olives = about 43.5 m³/ha/day; annual total 7,717 m³/ha. Source [36] · LowHow often: Daily, by evaporation (stated in source)
  • Task 6: Olive fly: check traps (yellow sticky and McPhail) weekly and renew the bait; fruit is susceptible from pit hardening. Source [56] [78] · MediumHow often: Weekly check (stated in source)
  • Task 7: Olive moth: monitor the second flight (May–June, fruit generation). Source [44] · MediumHow often: Weekly reading (set by compiler from source timing)
  • Task 8: Jasmine moth: flight period (May–June and September–November); mating disruption with pheromone at 80 g/ha, or Trichogramma releases of 9,000 per tree every two weeks, especially on young growth. Source [66] [84] · MediumHow often: Release every two weeks (stated in source)
  • Task 9: Olive psyllid: inspect for nymphs on shoots and inflorescences; one generation a year at Al-Arish: eggs laid in twig buds from November, nymphs from November/December to June–August, peak around mid-April; damage is raceme drop, pistil drying and honeydew; in Tunisia 6–8 insects per raceme caused 13% loss and over 30 insects more than 40%. Source [45] [46] · HighHow often: Not given in sources (not given in sources)
  • Task 10: Leopard moth: flight until early November; check traps and active galleries. Source [86] [47] · MediumHow often: Not given in sources (not given in sources)
  • Task 11: Verticillium wilt: summer thermal drone survey (20 cm resolution) to detect early infected trees from raised crown temperature and CWSI. Source [87] · HighHow often: Not given in sources (not given in sources)

13. Information Gaps (what the sources did not provide)

No reliable published value was found for these items; complete them with field measurements or by consulting the Horticulture Research Institute, the Desert Research Center or the certification body.

  1. Green table-olive harvest week for each variety in Egypt (Aggezi, Toffahi, green Manzanillo); only the international definition of the stage and Toffahi's early harvest are available.
  2. Black Kalamata harvest date in Egypt.
  3. Irrigation volumes measured on Egyptian desert land for each phase; available are the Haifa Mediterranean schedules, FAO coefficients and the February recommendation (twice a week).
  4. Timing and rate (kg/tree) of compost for bearing trees in Egypt.
  5. Planting-hole dimensions and irrigation rates for newly planted seedlings in Egypt.
  6. The list of organic inputs permitted under Law 12/2020 and the bio-products registered with the Agricultural Pesticide Committee.
  7. The Horticulture Research Institute variety map and descriptions of the registered selections.
  8. Chilling requirements of Egyptian varieties and flowering dates for each region.
  9. Olive fly action thresholds calibrated for Egypt, and thresholds for the psyllid and olive moth.
  10. Egyptian organic trials against the psyllid, bark beetle and peacock spot.
  11. Year of first fruiting for each variety on Egyptian land; available only is that cutting-grown trees bear fruit in about four years in general.
  12. Pages 24–69 of the ECOLIVE guide (organic fertilisation, oil extraction, diseases) were missing from the uploaded file.
